extracted.intended_audience: citizens, lawmakers, and readers interested in constitutional design and the powers of the Executive
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative arguments for structuring and evaluating the powers of a republican Executive (veto, command of military, pardons, treaty-making, appointments, judicial separation). Useful for assessing constitution design choices about executive authority and checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the Executive veto / negative
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary inducement to conferring the power in question upon the Executive is, to enable him to defend himself; the secondary one is to increase the chances in favor of the community against the passing of bad laws, through haste, inadvertence, or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veto power is justified not because the Executive is presumed wiser, but because legislatures are fallible and may be driven by faction, haste, or encroachment; more examination and diversity of viewpoints reduce errors. The veto helps guard against laws passed by contagion of passions or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative preferred to absolute negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of an absolute negative, it is proposed to give the Executive the qualified negative already described (return for reconsideration subject to final rejection only if more than one third of each house concur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualified negative is more readily exercised and less offensive in appearance, so it may be more effectual in practice. It encourages reconsideration and unites Executive objections with a respectable proportion of the legislature, avoiding the harshness of a categorical veto while retaining a check on bad laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk trade-off: veto may prevent good laws but favors stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of preventing bad laws includes that of preventing good ones; but the injury from defeating a few good laws is amply compensated by the advantage of preventing many bad ones and promoting stability in legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate veto power by weighing occasional suppression of beneficial measures against the greater public good of preventing frequent ill-considered or faction-driven statutes; favoring stability in the system of legislation is a key metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in Executive use of veto (low risk of abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The superior weight and influence of the legislative body and the hazard to the Executive in a trial of strength with that body afford a satisfactory security that the negative would generally be employed with great caution; there would oftener be room for a charge of timidity than of rashness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a clash with the legislature is risky for the Executive, expect self-restraint; empirical likelihood of abuse is low. Consider political costs/constraints as intrinsic checks when judging practical safety of veto power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judiciary from executive revisory roles
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to keep the judges too distinct from every other avocation than that of expounding the laws. It is peculiarly dangerous to place them in a situation to be either corrupted or influenced by the Executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutional arrangements that associate judges with executive revisory bodies (e.g., councils including judges to exercise executive negatives), because prior advisory roles or frequent association with the Executive risk biasing judicial interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief: war requires single-hand direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the cares or concerns of government, the direction of war most peculiarly demands those qualities which distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand. The direction of war implies the direction of the common strength; and the power of directing and employing the common strength forms a usual and essential part in the definition of the executive authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For military command, prioritize unity, secrecy, decision, and despatch; evaluate arrangements by whether they enable prompt, coherent direction of national force under a single accountable person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power: discretionary, humane, and vested in single Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be authorized to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment. Humanity and good policy dictate that the power of pardoning should be as little fettered or embarrassed as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pardoning power by its ability to temper severity in the criminal code, afford timely mercy, and operate without undue procedural delay; single-executive discretion is defended because it fosters scrupulousness and avoids collective obduracy or excessive clemency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and discretion of pardons in rebellions/insurrections
rubrics_metrics.description: In seasons of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments, when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquillity of the commonwealth; the dilatory process of convening the legislature would frequently be the occasion of letting slip the golden opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating who should hold pardon power, prioritize the capacity for immediate discretionary action in crises—delays for legislative sanction can be politically and practically fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on delegating pardon power and political optics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is questionable whether, in a limited Constitution, that power could be delegated by law; and it would generally be impolitic beforehand to take any step which might hold out the prospect of impunity. A proceeding out of the usual course would be construed into timidity or weakness and would embolden guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legal limits on delegation and the reputational/political effects of broad pre-authorizations to pardon; institutional design should avoid signals that encourage impunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making: joint power of President and Senate (two-thirds of members present)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur. Treaties are contracts with foreign nations which have the force of law and require both executive negotiation qualities and legislative participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties should combine Executive agency (diplomatic skill, secrecy, dispatch) with legislative assent because of their binding law-like effects. Evaluate treaty rules by whether they balance foreign respect and executive competence against safeguards against executive corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude House from treaty-making: reasons of secrecy, steadiness, and dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: The fluctuating and multitudinous composition of the House, and its tendency toward frequent calls and long convenings, make it incompatible with the qualities essential to treaty negotiations (accurate foreign knowledge, steady views, decision, secrecy, and despatch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging institutional participants in treaty power, favor smaller, more stable bodies that can act with necessary secrecy and continuity; inclusion of large/populous assemblies undermines effective foreign negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-thirds of members present better than two-thirds of whole body
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions which require more than the majority of any body to its resolutions have a direct tendency to embarrass the operations of the government. Requiring two thirds of all members would, in many cases from non-attendance, amount to a necessity of unanimity and produce impotence and disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design supermajority rules to apply to attending members rather than to entire membership to promote punctuality and avoid paralysis; historical precedents show excessive quorum/supermajority requirements cause inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointment: nomination by President with Senate advice and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is 'to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint' principal officers. Nomination vests the principal judgment in the President while Senate concurrence acts as a check against favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess appointment systems by their capacity to produce competent administration: single-nominee responsibility promotes careful selection, while legislative concurrence restrains nepotism, state prejudice, and purely partisan bargains. Consider practical likelihood of Senate rejection and the stabilizing psychological effect of possible rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of nomination+consent over sole appointment or assembly appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: One man of discernment is better fitted to analyze and estimate peculiar qualities for offices than a body; yet requiring the concurrence of the Senate adds a silent but powerful check against favoritism and instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating appointment regimes, weigh the virtues of concentrated responsibility (thorough candidate scrutiny, reputational incentives) against the corrective role of a confirming body to deter unfit appointments arising from personal attachments or party bargains.
